title: A Week In San Francisco On A $1,673,000 Joint Income
text:
A Week In San Francisco On A $1,673,000 Joint Income

Welcome to Money Diaries where we are tackling the ever-present taboo that is money. We’re asking real people how they spend their hard-earned money during a seven-day period — and we’re tracking every last dollar.

This week: An operations manager working in technology who makes $210,000 per year and spends some of it on a coffee grinder.

If you’d like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we’re not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.

This diary was written in 2026. This is a follow-up diary, you can read the previous diary here.

Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We’d love to hear your thoughts here.

Occupation: Operations
Industry: Technology
Age: 38
Location: San Francisco, CA
Salary: $210,000 salary plus $63,000 annual bonus (30%), and 5% ownership in RSUs.
Joint Income/Financial Setup: My husband, W.’s salary: $400,000 base plus $600,000 bonus (bonus is the average he has gotten over the last five years). We have a joint account that all of our expenses come out of.
Assets: $8M ($1.2M 401K, $4M investment accounts, $800K in various bank accounts, $2M equity in home).
Debt: $1M (loan on house)
Paycheck Amount (2x/month): $6,200 (and W’s is $11,000)
Pronouns: She/her

Monthly Expenses

Housing Costs:
Mortgage: $5,500
Loan Payments: $0
Health Insurance: $200
Internet/Cable/Security System: $400
Water/Sewer: ~$250 (depends on the month)
Electricity: ~$650
Garbage: $40
Netflix: $0 (share with family)
Cell Phone: $150
Spotify: $20
GCloud: $1.99
iCloud Storage: $2.99
Disney+: $7 (share with our families)
Donations: $500 (Planned Parenthood, Red Cross, American Heart Association, Habitat for Humanity, etc.)
Preschool: $3,000 (will be increasing to $5,000 for K. in the fall)
O.’s extra-curricular activities: $500
Undergraduate Donation: ~$2,000 annually
Homeowner’s Insurance: $2500 annually
Car Insurance: $2250 annually
Car Registration: $750 annually
Property Taxes: $29,000 annually
Amazon Prime: $119 annually
Chase Credit Card Fees: $795 annually
Amex Credit Card Fees: $795 annually

Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?
Yes. From a very young age, my parents were clear that college was an expectation, not a question. Education was a central value in our household and academic success was strongly emphasized. My parents paid for my undergraduate education and expenses. While I considered getting an MBA and applied, I never followed through on enrolling after deferring.

Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?
Due to my dad’s career, money was discussed openly and regularly in our household. My parents were transparent that we had a privileged upbringing. My parents both came from families where they didn’t have to budget or track spending, and I had a similar upbringing, as well. One consistent principle they emphasized was avoiding debt whenever possible and prioritizing financial stability and long-term planning.

What was your first job and why did you get it?
My first job was a summer internship in college at a financial services firm in NYC. I got the internship to build my resume. My parents paid for my summer expenses in NYC. I was a Resident Assistant in college and got paid for it. I invested the income from it and we ended up using it as part of our down payment for the house we bought in San Francisco.

Did you worry about money growing up?
No. My parents consistently provided for everything we needed and most things we wanted. We were aware that we grew up with the ability to not have to worry about our financial position. I got quite a bit of flak about calling myself upper middle class in my previous diary. I stand by that assessment — I compare myself to those who grew up in the same city and my neighbors. In the area where we lived, we were upper middle class, but for the rest of the broader US or global population, we were in the top 1%.

Do you worry about money now?
We don’t track our expenses or worry about what we are spending daily. In my last diary, I was concerned about the future, but over the last two years, we have significantly increased our assets. I worked for a tech company that had a successful IPO, and the company my husband works at has paid him well in the 10 years he has been there. Also, he has a large upside if he continues to perform well. If my husband and I maintain our current lifestyle, with minimal creep, we will be more than fine for the future.

At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?
I started being self-sufficient when I graduated from college and started my first professional full-time job. My parents and W.’s parents have been our safety nets since we graduated from college, but we were fortunate to never rely on them. Over time, we have noticed that my parents have been more generous with us than W.’s parents.

Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.
I received passive income in college to pay for expenses outside of room and board and tuition. This worked out to be about $20,000 over four years of college. My parents contributed $20,000 for my wedding, W.’s parents contributed $20,000 as well, and the remaining we covered. When our son was born, my parents gave me $25,000 and we used that to start a 529 for our son.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day One: Sunday

6 a.m. — My son, O., wakes up and calls for my husband, W., so he gets him up. He then comes to my side of the bed to wake me up. We have about 15 people from W.’s company (10 adults and five kids) coming over for brunch and it’s all O. is talking about.

9 a.m. — We have spent the last three hours prepping for the brunch — asparagus frittata, chocolate chip pancake, breakfast potatoes, croissants with lavender blueberry jam, citrus salad, bacon, granola parfaits, cinnamon rolls, and fresh fruit. O. helps me squeeze orange juice for the mimosas. $353.73

10 a.m. — Folks have started arriving and we spend the next three-ish hours entertaining the kids and adults. It was great meeting everyone and their families. O. does an incredible job being a gracious host and sharing his toys. I’m super thankful that we are left with minimal leftovers.

1 p.m. — O., W., and I tidy up the living room, dining room, and kitchen. O. goes down for his afternoon nap. He only naps on the weekends since he is at home. At school, he suffers from FOMO and doesn’t nap anymore.

3 p.m. — O. wakes up from his nap and we decide to go to the park since it’s such a beautiful day in SF. It is over 70 degrees and the park isn’t too far. O. and I ride his scooter to the park while W. stays home to work.

5 p.m. — At the park, we happen to run into one of his classmates from preschool. I love when we see friends there because O. then hangs out with them rather than asking me to play with him the entire time. The other kid’s parents and I socialize and watch the kids play together.

6 p.m. — O., W., and I head to O.’s swimming class. O. has a ritual where he goes to the local taqueria for tacos and then goes to his swimming lesson. W. gets some fajitas but I’m not craving Mexican food and skip. O. has been taking swimming lessons for a year and we have seen a huge improvement in his abilities over that time. $57

8 p.m. — We return home after the lesson. We get O. ready for bed — shower, brush teeth, stories, night light/white noise, and he’s in his bed.

10 p.m. — I watch an episode of The Real Housewives of SLC and sleep. It’s always interesting to watch the show when it was shot sometimes a year plus ago, and you know that some major things have happened since then.

Daily Total: $410.73

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Two: Monday

7 a.m. — Ever since the time change, O. sleeps in and wakes up an hour later. W. is already downstairs making coffee for himself. O. grabs me from bed and we head downstairs to get ready for preschool. I make him some eggs, a toasted bagel, bacon, and cut him some berries. He eats most of it and gets ready for school.

9 a.m. — I drop O. off at school and head to my desk to work. When I come home, I notice that W. has left for work. I’m lucky to have a job that is fully remote/virtual. It gives me the flexibility to start working after I drop off O. at school without having to worry about a commute to an office.

10 a.m. — I try to catch up on any open items that might have come in over the weekend. I shared my Calendly link for the various candidate interviews I have and ended up with over 20 hours of interviews this week. Definitely didn’t do a good job spacing out the interviews.

12 p.m. — I have a new hire starting today and after his orientation this morning, he is finally logged in, so I meet with him and walk him through his onboarding plan, including his 30/60/90 day expectations. I’m excited to have him after three months of searching for the right person. The two of us end our call and join our weekly team meeting. I quickly make some noodle soup with tofu, veggies, noodles, and coconut peanut broth I have in the fridge. I eat it during the team meeting.

3 p.m. — I spend the afternoon doing more interviews. I’m thankful when a candidate sends me a message that she needs to reschedule. I meet with my new hire again to check in on how onboarding is going. I’m blown away by how quickly he is picking things up and how much of a self-starter he is.

5 p.m. — I pick up O. from school and take him to his soccer class. O. is eating a sandwich in the car. On our way to soccer, we have a bathroom emergency so need to make a pit stop at home. We’re a few minutes late to soccer but since it is our first class of the season, the class hasn’t started yet. Also, this is toddler soccer so no sweat.

6 p.m. — O. finishes soccer and heads to the playground attached to the field. W. is waiting for us there. W. brought some pizza from a local restaurant we like. I say bye to O. so I can head to my monthly book club. $62

9 p.m. — The book club is at another lady’s house and she has a beautiful view of the SF skyline. The entire time we are at the book club, I’m gawking at both how clear it is and that I can see everything from the Golden Gate Bridge to the Palace of Fine Arts to Alcatraz from her living room. I like that this book club is low pressure — I didn’t get to read the book from last month. I bring along a bottle of red wine, crackers, and cheese. $46.50

10 p.m. — I watch an episode of Love is Blind and sleep. Again, it is already public knowledge that one of the couples is divorced after only being married for a few months, so it feels anti-climactic to watch the wedding when I know what has happened. As you will probably see, I watch a lot of reality TV. I feel like my life is so boring and mundane that I love seeing the drama that reality TV has.

Daily Total: $108.50

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Three: Tuesday

7 a.m. — Similar morning ritual every day — O. wakes up and grabs me. We head downstairs and I make him a croissant sandwich filled with Nutella and fruit. He eats most of it, plays a bit with his Lego, and gets ready for school.

9 a.m. — I drop O. off at school and head to my desk to work. I stop by the plant store to buy three plants, and the grocery store too to buy some more fruit. I don’t have enough time before my first meeting to buy everything on the grocery list. I spend the first hour checking in with my new hire and making sure he has everything he needs. I check my email and see that we got into one of the private schools we applied for. It’s a relief to know that we don’t have to move. $72

10 a.m. — I get an alert from one of our employees that the direct deposits for the entire team didn’t get deposited today. I start scrambling with various team members to get an update and resolve the issue, while also attending an interview where the candidate is doing a presentation.

12 p.m. — We still haven’t resolved the payroll issue. Multiple members of the leadership team have weighed in on this and the Slack thread is now 76 messages over two hours. There isn’t a DRI [Designated Responsible Individual] who owns this. I’m going to let someone else dictate messaging here since I don’t agree with the decision being made. I make a quick egg scramble with veggies and toast. I’m trying to be good about incorporating more protein into my meals.

3 p.m. — I spend the afternoon doing more interviews. I’m monitoring responses from some of the folks who didn’t get paid, and understandably they’re very agitated.

5 p.m. — Before heading to pick up O. from school, I send a message to the team saying I think the responses to the employees lack empathy and we should regroup in the morning to talk about how we respond.

6 p.m. — O. and W. eat dinner. I didn’t have much time to prep today so I make some ravioli with pesto, veggies, and chicken for dinner. I decide to go for a run so I can clear my head. The weather in SF is beautiful in the spring. I’m loving that it’s brighter in the evenings.

8 p.m. — W. folds laundry, while I do dishes from dinner. O. is playing with his Lego. O. goes to bed, and I message a friend who I’m supposed to grab lunch with tomorrow about when and where we’re meeting. I don’t have the energy tonight to watch TV, so I call it an early night.

Daily Total: $72

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Four: Wednesday

7 a.m. — Similar morning ritual every day — O. wakes up and grabs me. We head downstairs and I make him a pulled pork sandwich with Hawaiian rolls and cucumbers. O. isn’t always into breakfast food so sometimes I make him lunch/dinner meals for breakfast. He eats most of it, plays a bit with his Magna-Tiles, and gets ready for school. On Wednesdays, he doesn’t like the lunch his school provides him so I make him a deli sandwich with turkey, salami, and sopressata on Dave’s Killer Bread.

9 a.m. — I drop O. off at school and head to my desk to work. I stop by the dry cleaners to pick up W.’s shirts ($22) and go to Trader Joe’s to buy our weekly groceries ($147.52). I also happen to go to Whole Foods to buy coffee for W. ($52.61). I liked this Whole Foods since they have a coffee grinder. Only to find out that they got rid of it as well, so I will now have to buy a coffee grinder. I spend the first hour checking in with my new hire and making sure he has everything he needs for the day. $222.13

10 a.m. — I spend the next two hours conducting interviews for candidates. I used to try to mute my Slack and email notifications, but have realized it makes me miss supporting my team. I find it so hard to be present during an interview while also ensuring the broader business has the support they need for escalations.

12 p.m. — I meet a friend, M., for lunch. It’s beautiful weather and we sit outside. I get a plate with rice, beans, salsa, avocados, and a yummy chipotle sauce. They have a delicious watermelon agua fresca I usually get but I have been trying to cut down on my sugar and lately haven’t been craving anything sweet. I have a great time catching up with my friend. She updates me on her work, personal life, and job search. She just ran an ultramarathon, so I hear all about that. We used to work together about 10 years ago, and she is one of my closest confidantes. In a remote work environment, I haven’t been able to make the same quality of friends as when I was in an office. $32.67

3 p.m. — I spend the afternoon doing more interviews. In between interviews, I help review some SOPs my team created, provide feedback on some open items and start creating a product request I have for our Engineering Team.

5 p.m. — I meet one more time with my new hire to check in, answer any questions, and give him some context about the meetings he will have tomorrow. W. comes home and we catch up about our days before heading to pick up O. from school. I also buy a De’Longhi burr coffee grinder. $119.95

6 p.m. — O. and W. eat dinner. I made a rack of ribs and grilled some corn for them. I head out to an art gallery opening I got tickets for. I meet a friend who is joining me. The wife is a painter while the husband is the musician. It’s really nice to see both together and how each of their works ties together.

9 p.m. — I head home after the event and O. is already asleep. W. is working in his office so I pop in to say hi. I appreciate that O. and W. cleaned up after dinner, started the dishwasher, and swept the floors so I don’t have any household tasks I need to do. I watch an episode of Shark Tank. I like all of the new guest judges. It reminds me that I couldn’t be an entrepreneur. I enjoy being a cog in the machine at a company.

Daily Total: $374.75

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Five: Thursday

7 a.m. — Similar morning ritual every day — O. wakes up and grabs me. We head downstairs and he just wants the leftovers from yesterday night’s dinner: ribs and corn. He finishes it all and asks for more. I don’t have more so I offer him other options and he picks eating strawberries while playing with his cars. I make my tea for the morning and get ready for drop-off.

9 a.m. — I check the portal and find out that W. got into another school. This school is low on our list, so we still prefer the one we heard back from on Tuesday. I cancel my morning check-in with my new hire, so I can spend some focused time on creating the product request before my first candidate interview.

10 a.m. — I spend the next two hours conducting interviews for candidates. I get alerted that one of the people who did not get paid wants to set up time with me to chat. She says she is available at 12 p.m., which is perfect since it’s when I’m free as well.

12 p.m. — I speak to the person who didn’t get paid. She asks me if I’m confident that she will get paid tomorrow. I’m transparent with her that I confirmed with the vendor that she will be and we should definitely check in tomorrow to ensure that it happened. She is much more understanding than I would be if I didn’t get paid, so I appreciate it. I eat my leftover rice plate after I hang up with her before my 12:30 p.m. meeting. I log into the portal a final time and find out that we got into the last two schools. We feel so fortunate to have so many choices and need to spend the next few days assessing our options.

3 p.m. — I spend the afternoon having our weekly meetings. We have one with cross-functional partners. We have our team meeting as well. I check in with the team and make sure I address any questions or concerns they have. They remind me of a couple of open projects that they need my guidance on, so I provide real-time responses. My team is great at staying on top of things and does an incredible job with all of the moving pieces we have.

5 p.m. — I do my daily check-in with my new hire. W. comes home with O. and I make them dinner. Tonight is chicken burritos with veggies, Spanish rice, and black beans. O. likes them deconstructed so he can do it himself. W. actually uses a soft taco-size tortilla since it makes it more manageable for him to hold it. We spend the rest of the evening before bedtime doing puzzles, painting some papers with watercolors, and listening to stories on Alexa.

9 p.m. — O. goes to sleep and I get ready for bed as well. I spend an hour reading the book for my book club, All The Other Mothers Hate Me by Sarah Harman. I can’t say I’m surprised this was the pick since we are all mothers! This book is great. It’s an easy read and the main character is everything I strive not to be as a mother. I start getting tired so I call it a night around 10:30 p.m.

Daily Total: $0

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Six: Friday

7 a.m. — Similar morning ritual every day — O. wakes up and grabs me. We head downstairs and he eats hash browns, scrambled eggs, toast, and some sliced oranges. Today our cleaning lady comes, so O. is responsible for putting all his toys away before school. On Fridays, he does not like the lunch his school provides him, so I make him spinach ravioli in pesto sauce and put it into a thermos. I appreciate that the school is open to me providing lunch on days he doesn’t like what is on the menu.

9 a.m. — I spend the morning in meetings. I’m glad this super heavy meeting week is coming to an end. We have our hour-long weekly business review, followed by a meeting with the product/eng team on priorities. I spend the next two hours in candidate interviews and responding to Slack and email escalations. Our cleaning lady has a key to the house so she lets herself in at some point. $140

12 p.m. — I take a quick break to go get my car washed and a walk around the neighborhood while it is being done. $50

1 p.m. — I spend the afternoon trying to get organized for next week — determining any open items that I need to close out on for today, prioritizing what I need to work on for next week and updating my various weekly 1:1s with my direct reports about what projects they will need to work on. I take a break to eat some fried rice with tofu that I make.

5 p.m. — W. comes home with O. and we go to a local Italian place for dinner. Friday is a night I try not to cook and we usually go to a restaurant. We order a mushroom pasta, lasagna and a lamb ragu pasta. $117

8 p.m. — O. goes to bed and I need to respond to some emails and text messages from friends. I try so hard to put my phone away, but randomly I will notice I’m doom scrolling. I spend a little time reading my book as well before calling it a night early at 9:45 p.m.

Daily Total: $307

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Seven: Saturday

7 a.m. — O. wakes up and jumps into our bed to shake W. awake. After some silly games like I Spy, we all head downstairs to start our morning.

8 a.m. — W. and O. usually go to get bagels and the farmers’ market. They each get a bagel with butter and a side of pastrami ($14) and buy some fruit from the farmers’ market ($16). I decide to skip today so I get some things done at home. $30

10 a.m. — O. is back home and anxiously awaiting for his friends to arrive for his playdate. Unfortunately, his friends are late and we end up playing tag on the street while waiting for them to arrive. They arrive around 10:30.

12 p.m. — The five kids have a blast playing with the trucks, trains, and other toys we have at our house. The moms hang out on the couch just catching up. All of the kids are going to start Kindergarten in fall, so we spend a majority of the time discussing where we got in and what we anticipate doing. We all eat spaghetti and meatballs with a choice of berries and cucumber or carrots for lunch.

2 p.m. — All the kids leave, we clean up and O. takes his nap for the next 90 minutes. I prep for the crispy pan pizza I’m making for dinner and rest for a bit as well.

4 p.m. — After O. wakes up, I take him to get his hair cut. After over five years, I have finally talked him into going to the salon. I was doing a terrible job with the razor and I’m so happy to have a professional cut his hair. $47

5 p.m. — I put the pizza in the oven and spend the time while it is in the oven to power wash the stairs. It feels so satisfying to see the stairs free of dirt and moss. The pizza comes out delicious and golden brown. I serve everyone some pizza. I go back to power washing after dinner.

8 p.m. — O. starts complaining that he is itchy. I assume it is from the haircut even though we rinsed off after the haircut. After almost 90 minutes of stalling, he finally falls asleep in his bed.

10 p.m. — I watch the reunion episode of Love is Blind (season 10). W. and I try to talk about which school we like. Our top two schools are in opposite directions from where we live, so logistically the same one is more academically driven, which is the one W. prefers, and I prefer the other one because it seems more like a community. We’re at an impasse and have another 48 hours to decide. I get tired and go to bed.

Daily Total: $77

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Breakdown

Conclusion:
I realized that while I didn’t have any major big-ticket purchases, I had a lot of everyday purchases and spending to maintain our household. In my previous diary, I booked travel and a trip, which I considered our big-ticket item. It felt like a good mix of time alone, time with friends and family, and time running errands. I feel like our family spending is mostly around how to make my family and my life easier and run smoothly.

title: Iris Chacón Helped Me (& Generations of Women) Challenge Colonial Ideas About Power, Freedom, & Beauty
text:
Iris Chacón Helped Me (& Generations of Women) Challenge Colonial Ideas About Power, Freedom, & Beauty

I’ve always been fascinated by showgirls, often exploring the history of Latin American and Caribbean vedettes and their cultural influence throughout my journalism career. I think it’s because, from as early as I can remember, they made me rethink so much of what I had been taught about beauty and freedom. Growing up as a shy, modest, chubby girl in the 1990s and early 2000s, an era when glossy magazines circled curvy women’s thighs in red ink, these dazzling performers from another time seemed untouched by that shame.

They weren’t just baring their skin on stage. They treated their bodies as works of art, adorning them with sequins, feathers, and rhinestones, as they commanded attention with their dance, humor, and sensuality. They reveled in being seen, making visibility seem less like vulnerability and more like power. I didn’t have the language for it then, but I wanted whatever freedom they possessed.

As a Puerto Rican girl, no one captivated me more than Iris Chacón, the illustrious vedette who rose to fame in San Juan in the 1970s and became one of the earliest woman cross-over artists. “La Vedette de América,” as she’s been nicknamed, produced and hosted her own weekly hit variety TV show “El Show de Iris Chacón” for more than a decade, reaching No. 1 ratings in Puerto Rico and airing in U.S. markets like New York, Chicago, Miami, and Los Angeles. The “Bombshell of Puerto Rico” had monthslong residencies over multiple years at the iconic Caribe Hilton, lighting up the stage at Club Caribe, the hotel’s legendary cabaret showroom. There, she became part of the same glamorous legacy that drew stars like Elizabeth Taylor, Sophia Loren, and Rita Moreno to the resort. 

Iris was also the first Latine artist to sell out performances at New York’s Radio City Music Hall in the ‘70s and was photographed by the iconic fashion illustrator Antonio Lopez in Andy Warhol’s Interview Magazine.

By the time I was coming of age in the early millennium, the height of her fame had passed, but she remained a cultural icon — one that is still celebrated today. In fact, in the spring of 2026, Caribe Hilton opened a permanent on-site exhibit reflecting the hotel’s history – from its grand opening in 1949 to the birth of the piña colada in 1954 to Iris’ revered performances in the ‘80s, which sold out to crowds made up of both local Puerto Ricans and tourists alike. Meanwhile, in May, Iris, now 76, returned to Puerto Rico for two sold-out performances of Las Noches del Caribe at Moneró Café Teatro & Bar in Caguas. Inspired by her legendary cabaret residencies, the intimate production recreated the glamour and spectacle of Puerto Rico’s golden age of hotel showgirl entertainment.

But for Puerto Rican women — and for Latina viewers across the world — Iris was more than an amusing pastime or barrier-breaker. She gave women permission to push past the gendered rules that constrained them, reject the false choice between purity and sensuality, embrace their bodies with confidence, and imagine a freer way of moving through the world. And as showgirl culture — in the form of burlesque, drag, and traditional vedettes — re-emerge in Puerto Rico, she is inspiring a new generation. 

For American Colony, a podcast from The Latino Newsletter and Shake It Easy Media, I trace Iris’ extraordinary legacy and how she transformed fame and entertainment into tools for challenging colonial ideas about power, femininity, and visibility. In my episode “La Chacón,” produced alongside Locatora Productions’ Diosa Femme and Mala Muñoz, I explore how both Puerto Rico and showgirls have been commoditized and consumed as exotic paradises, and how Iris manipulated the imperial script to build creative independence, employ women and queer artists, and expand what generations of Puerto Rican women imagined was possible for their bodies and their lives.

title: Gap Just Brought Back Its Fragrance Collection — & Made It Better
text:
Gap Just Brought Back Its Fragrance Collection — & Made It Better

Before brands like Le Labo and Sol de Janeiro became beauty-industry obsessions, the cult-favorite scents of the mall generation came from the same place as your go-to jeans: Gap. Back in the day, Dream, Heaven, Grass, and Om weren’t just random nouns — they were Gap’s bestselling perfume collection. And after years off shelves, the iconic fragrances have been reimagined for a new generation of beauty lovers.

Created by renowned DSM-Firmenich perfumers Honorine Blanc (who worked on the original fragrances) and Nicole Mancini, the collection includes refreshed versions of the four original scents, along with one brand-new addition: Harmony.  

As a fragrance lover and proud ’90s baby, I couldn’t wait to get my nose on them. Ahead, I put the entire lineup to the test to see whether these affordable, nostalgic fragrances still hold up — and which ones are actually worth adding to your perfume wardrobe. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Heaven

Heaven made me do a double take (or should I say double sniff?) on first spritz. If I hadn’t seen the Gap bottle with my own eyes, I would’ve guessed it came from another mall fragrance mainstay: Victoria’s Secret. Although it’s technically a floral amber (a family that pairs romantic florals with warm, resinous notes like amber, ambrox, and tonka bean), the dessert-like vanilla is what really shines on my skin. It’s sweet, sexy, and surprisingly sophisticated. Alongside Madagascar vanilla, you’ll find juicy pear and honeysuckle, while patchouli and musk anchor the fragrance with a sensual, skin-like finish. I found myself reaching for this one most often for date nights and girls’ nights out, and love how it stayed on my hair and clothes especially.  

Grass

On paper, Grass is closest to the types of fragrances I naturally gravitate toward. I love a crisp, herbaceous scent for daytime, especially in the summer, so its clean, citrus-forward profile had me convinced it’d be my favorite of the bunch. (It’s also the only original Gap fragrance I’d ever tried, and I remember loving it as a kid.) Rather than recreating the original note-for-note, Grass offers a more modern interpretation, opening with invigorating green mandarin and violet leaf before unfolding into woody cypress, creamy matcha, and a grounding blend of earthy cedar and bright vetiver. The result is a unique, long-lasting fragrance that strikes a beautiful balance between freshly showered skin and milky green tea. Of the five, this also felt the most gender-neutral; I loved it just as much on my husband as I did on myself. 

Dream

Next up, Dream. As the name suggests, this feminine floral musk is utterly romantic. Right away, I picked up sparkling bergamot, neroli, and orange blossom. That citrusy trio gives way to a bouquet of jasmine and freesia before settling into a base of cedarwood, soft musk, and warm amber. It’s pretty, airy, and undeniably feminine, but ultimately not for me. I don’t typically gravitate toward sweeter florals, but if that’s your fragrance love language, this would make a lovely addition to your perfume wardrobe.

Om

I won’t bury the lede here: Om is my clear favorite of the bunch. It has an effortlessly cozy, skin-like quality where no single note steals the spotlight — everything simply works together. The woody aromatic fragrance opens with bright ginger and smoky olibanum (a beloved note of mine that also appears in Lore’s Somewhere but Nowhere, one of my most reached-for perfumes) before settling into warm sandalwood and herbal coriander flower. Amber woods, velvety cashmeran, and cedar create a comforting, lingering dry down that feels tailor-made for fall. I’ve barely stopped wearing it since it arrived, and despite its impressive longevity, it never feels overpowering — just like you naturally smell amazing. 

Harmony

Last but not least, there’s Harmony. Unlike the previous scents, Harmony is a brand-new addition to Gap’s fragrance portfolio. The fruity floral has top notes of bright bergamot and juicy apricot nectar, before revealing a bouquet of sweet white florals — gardenia, jasmine, and tuberose, and a base of sheer woods and warm amber. My first impressions of this one were that it’s fresh and fruity, but not in a teeny-bopper way. Perhaps this is controversial, but I’m calling it now: This is the perfect gym perfume because it’s light and clean, and not super strong. To be honest, I felt like this one didn’t last as long as the other Gap scents, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing, as it allows me to layer it with others without getting overpowering or simply have it fade if I want to wear fragrance but not worry about it causing someone a headache.

text:
The Unexpected Detail Making Bermuda Shorts Look So Much Cooler

It’s no secret by now that Bermuda shorts are having quite the moment. Whether it’s a relaxed denim fit or a perfectly polished linen option, the modest length has never felt cooler. Now, Copenhagen’s brightest street style stars are taking them to the next level, opting for camouflage-covered designs to make their front-row-ready outfits pop.

Yes, the pattern that was once reserved for troops is inching its way back to the top of fashion charts. The beauty of the print is that it almost acts as a neutral in your wardrobe and can be worn in so many different ways. Don’t take my word for it. Just look at the plethora of looks that included the motif on day one of Copenhagen Fashion Week Spring/Summer ’27.

Josefien Weyns made her camo outfit standout amongst the crowd of show goers by pairing the shorts with a textured top and red accessories. If you’re going out or looking for a way to elevate yours, cherry heels and a coordinating bag bring the shorts into dressier territory.

On the other side of the spectrum, your favorite T-shirt and go-to flats work just as well for chill moments. Bonus points if you zhuzh up the look with cool shades, an on-the-go tote bag, and a pair of Maison Margiela Tabis.

I know fall is right around the corner. But there’s no need to pack up your Bermuda shorts just yet. Another street style star showed us how to keep the look going strong by styling her camo shorts with a long-sleeve button-down shirt layered under an oversized tee. It’s a transitional outfit idea to bookmark for the unpredictable weather ahead.

Similarly, a buttery cardigan will get the job done as well. Thong kitten heels add a modern cool factor, while a pair of skinny sunnies gives it that Matrix aura.

Camo Bermuda shorts might be the secret to ensuring every outfit looks instantly cool. Thanks, Copenhagen, for the sartorial cheat code.

title: Influencer Haley Baylee Takes Us Inside Old Navy’s Campaign & Under-$50 Fall Denim Collection
text:
Influencer Haley Baylee Takes Us Inside Old Navy’s Campaign & Under-$50 Fall Denim Collection

Coming off the back of a star-studded summer campaign with Paris Hilton, Ciara Miller, and Rob Rausch, Old Navy has brought back the iconic “It’s Old Navy” series for fall. And with a statement cast of Cardi B, Paloma Elsesser, Brooks Nader, Quenlin Blackwell, Haley Baylee, and Wisdom Kaye, we’re hooked again. The celebrities, models, and influencers showcase the fall’s “Most Wanted Denim” lineup in a cinematic Wild West video full of drama and humor, officially debuting on August 5.

“This campaign celebrates the enduring spirit of American denim with bold silhouettes, bold personalities, unmistakable style, and the belief that everyone deserves great denim at an incredible value,” said Old Navy’s chief creative officer Zac Posen in a press release.

Highlighting curves and volume, the lineup includes the all-new Arc Jean, which is the brand’s modern approach to a barrel style, plus returning favorites like the High-Rise Wide Leg, Baggy Barrel, and Low-Rise Baggy Jeans starting as low as $22. (So if you didn’t get your hands on the viral Hailey Bieber’s Gap jeans… this is your next best chance to update your denim collection with celebrity-approved styles.)

To go behind the scenes of the campaign, Refinery29 spoke to Haley Baylee (aka Haley Kalil). You likely know the influencer and model from her satirical TikToks, Glambot red carpet videos, Sports Illustrated photoshoots, or the TIME100’s Creators list. And now, she’s in her first-ever Old Navy campaign, so she’s sharing her longtime love of the brand, experience on set, favorite denim style, and how she’s styling it for fall. Read the full interview and shop Old Navy styles ahead.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Refinery29: How does it feel to star in an Old Navy campaign? Have you been a longtime fan of Old Navy? Did you wear it as a child?

HK: Oh yeah. I mean, I grew up, not to put an age on myself, but I’m 33, so I grew up watching Old Navy campaigns play on my TV! And they were always so iconic. They had this iconic celebrity of the moment. It was always fun and bright and cool.

It’s where I got all my sweaters from when I went to school. It’s like you knew that school was starting when you’d see the Old Navy sweater and jean campaigns drop for fall. I grew up watching Old Navy campaigns, grew up idolizing Old Navy, grew up wearing Old Navy. So now to see myself in a campaign with somebody like Cardi B… I mean, it’s insane. It’s actually insane.

R29: Is there a specific Old Navy piece you remember having as a child? Was there a specific sweater design you loved?

HK: I had this bright blue sweater. I could probably find me in it. I’ll have to ask my mom because I’m actually at my mom’s house right now. But it was this bright blue sweater with a collar that was a little thicker, and it had stripes on it. And I was obsessed with it. I wore it all the time.

R29: You mentioned Cardi. It’s a very star-studded campaign. Was there anyone in particular you were really excited to meet or work with on the campaign?

HK: I’m obsessed with Cardi, of course. She was the number one, because not only is she beautiful, but she’s hilarious. But I’ve known Wisdom for quite a long time. So Wisdom and I have worked together on projects before, and I was excited to work with him again. And then I had never met Quen before. I was really excited to meet Quen because I watch her cooking show and I think she’s such a baddie. So I was just really excited to work with her. She’s fantastic.

R29: Did you have a favorite part of shooting the campaign?

HK: During the campaign, they had Wisdom and I in a scene together where we were running back and forth, stealing the jeans from this small little window like Bonnie and Clyde. And we just had a blast. We were in there, we were yapping inside and they’d be like: “Action.” And we’d run out, we’d grab the jeans, then we’d run back inside. We’d yap with each other in there. It was just fun. It felt like you were a kid on set.

R29: The fall collection highlights a lot of new and updated denim styles. Were there any that were your favorite silhouette, and why?

HK: Oh, the baggy. Definitely, definitely the low-rise baggy. If you see any of my content, you know that I’m usually in low rise. It just fits my body better. It also just feels like you’re wearing pajamas. These were the perfect low rise because they don’t come up too high. Some people make a low rise and they’re not actually low rise; they’re like mid-rise. And I’m like: “No, it’s not hitting on the hips!” This one is an actual low rise. And if you want the really, really intense boyfriend fit, just size up. When I was doing my fitting, I sized up and it was the perfect amount of baggy.

R29: Do you have any tips for styling low-rise jeans? What tops do you like to pair them with?

HK: It really depends on your personal style. Mine is a mix, I would say, between sometimes a little feminine, but I prefer to be a little more boyish in the way that I dress. So if I’m just feeling like I want to drown in my clothes, which I love, I’ll do a big baggy T-shirt, like a graphic tee. And then I’ll do a baggy jean, maybe a little belt, and you could tuck a part of the shirt in if you wanted to.

Or I love a cropped tank top with a low-rise baggy jean so that you have a little distance between the pant and the end of the top. It’s enough to showcase your figure while still being comfortable.

R29: What is your go-to fall outfit formula?

HK: Ooh, again, I’m such a comfy person. I just like being comfy. I feel like clothes that are too tight can overstimulate me. I’ll start picking at them and playing with them, and then I’ll just want to go home and change. So, finding the balance between fashion and comfort has been something that I’m still obviously trying to navigate. As you see, I wear a lot of sweatpants when I’m filming.

But I think it’s the low-rise baggy jeans because then they’re not tight on your skin paired with a really nice boot. I think that that can always elevate it. And then a really, really nice leather jacket. I love a leather jacket that’s a little bit tight in the waist, but a little baggy on the sleeves and shoulders. So then you get that really pretty triangular fit, and then your baggy pants add the volume on the bottom again. It just looks really nice. It also makes you look tall!

R29: As a fashion girlie, you’re very into really bold statements. Which fashion trend are you excited to try for the fall season?

HK: It’s crazy. I never thought that this would come back, but I guess fashion is all circular. All of the stuff that I wore when I was a kid is coming back around. You’re getting the jellies, you’re getting the baby doll tops. When I saw that 2016 triangle bikini on Love Island, I was like: “Oh my gosh, it’s all coming back.” All the things that I used to wear, like the Juicy Couture tracksuits, the Uggs… that kind of mall culture-y vibe is coming back. And I’m stoked because I have some vintage pieces from then that I’m really excited to whip out of my closet.

My mom used to always tell me: “If you keep things long enough, they will come back into style.” And I used to not believe her because I was like: “What do you mean? Style’s always going to be improving.” No, it all comes back around… just in a little bit of a different way. So it’s really fun to see. And I’m like: “Oh, I know how to dress like this because I dressed like this when I was 14!”

title: 9 Everyday Habits Of People Who Always Smell Good
text:
9 Everyday Habits Of People Who Always Smell Good

Everyone knows someone — a friend, cousin, or colleague — who always smells amazing. It could be the height of summer, when everyone else has melted into a sweaty puddle, but they somehow still smell fresh, like they’ve just emerged from a pile of clean laundry. You can’t quite put your finger on it. Is it their perfume? Their hair? Their clothes? Or all of the above?

We couldn’t figure it out either, so we asked the people who know a thing or two about smelling good: scent experts and enthusiasts, fragrance content creators, and esteemed perfumers.

Ahead, they share the habits and tricks they swear by to smell incredible — and none of them involve spending a small fortune on a niche fragrance that’s impossible to track down.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Exfoliating toner — under your armpits

Aamna Lone, a fragrance expert and content creator behind @perfumeconnoisseurz on Instagram, swears by using Paula’s Choice 6% Mandelic + 2% Lactic Acid AHA Liquid Exfoliant under her arms three times a week to help keep body odor at bay — alongside wearing an antiperspirant and choosing lightweight, 100% cotton shirts. “It sounds odd, but the toner lowers the pH of the skin in the underarm area, so the bacteria that feed on compounds in sweat are reduced,” says Lone. “I find that my body odor is noticeably less when I do this.”

Solid perfume on the ends of your hair

Hair perfume has its place, but Lush fragrance category lead Lee Howes makes a case for solid perfume — especially those containing moisturizing jojoba oil, candelilla wax, and castor oil, which Howes says are suitable for the ends of the hair. These are ingredients commonly found in hair oils and split-end serums, too. “Take your Lush solid perfume, apply a small amount of product onto your fingertips and gently massage into the ends of your hair to get wafts of scent every time your hair moves around you,” says Howes. Our favorite is Chelsea Morning, an equally zingy and buttery caramel citrus.

Layering two versions of the same scent

Fragrance content creator Habiba Suleiman-Adejoh, aka @femmescents on Instagram, is convinced that it’s the year of the body mist, which she says is an “easy way to create an effortless all-round scent cloud that follows you throughout the day.” But the key to maximizing its power is choosing a shower oil with similar notes. “Layering your scent in the shower, and then applying it on your skin, really helps it linger, so when you hug someone, they think, She smells really nice, without it even seeming like you are trying; it’s just effortless. Suleiman-Adejoh loves Glossier Sandstone Body & Hair Fragrance Mist layered with Sandstone Daily Oil Wash. “Together, they smell super chic and clean — a memorable your-skin-but-better type of scent,” she says.

Secret scent spots

“Besides my wrists, décolletage, and collarbone, I apply fragrance behind my ears, on the back of my neck, and even my inner thighs,” says Cherry Cheng, perfumer and founder of Jouissance Parfums. “These are places where the scent feels intimate and only available by invitation,” she adds. In fact, Cheng believes there’s a connection between scent, mood, and the body. “When you associate fragrance with pleasure and self-care, you naturally become more aware of how you move through the world,” she says. “To me, that’s what makes someone smell amazing — not just the perfume itself, but the habit of consistent self-care, as well as confidence and ease that come with wearing scents for your own enjoyment,” Cheng continues.

Perfume behind your knees

Lone loves to spray her trousers or skirts, so that when she walks, the movement of the fabric wafts a delicate plume of scent into the air. But what if you’re wearing something shorter? “To create a trail of scent in warmer weather, a couple of spritzes of your favorite perfume behind your knees can be really effective,” says Howes. “That’s because the skin is often warmer here and can help leave a trail of fragrance behind you.” He adds that if you’re sitting in a bar or restaurant, your fragrance will gently rise up, rather than creating a cloud of scent around you — and everyone else.

Wearing perfume to bed

“Because I work in fragrance, I rarely wear perfume during the day anymore,” says Cheng, “so by the evening, I want to wear perfume purely for myself.” One of her favorite rituals is spraying either side of her collarbones before she gets into bed. “I catch little wafts of it as I’m falling asleep, and the quiet promise of romance and pleasure, whether rooted in memories or imagination, brings me so much joy,” she says. “When fragrance becomes part of your daily rituals, you start to carry yourself differently.”

The unexpected power of powder

If you thought solid perfume was cool, you’ll love scented powders, says Howes, who sees them as an inexpensive way to fragrance the skin post-shower — especially if body lotions feel sticky or overwhelming. “Dusting powders offer a subtle yet beautiful way of bringing more scent into your routine,” says Howes. “After a shower or bath, dry the skin before gently dusting your powder onto arms, legs, or anywhere the skin will be bare for a soft scent cloud around you all day.” Try the Dusting Powder in Super Milk, a musky fragrance with hints of vanilla and coconut.

Smelling good starts in the shower

“My greatest tip for smelling great naturally — and feeling great, too — is to start with a fragranced body wash in the shower,” says Linda G. Levy, president of The Fragrance Foundation, who currently loves Aesop Geranium Leaf Body Cleanser and Body Balm. But the real secret to making the scent last is layering. “For staying power, fragrance is best applied to moist skin, so I smooth the matching body lotion or cream all over as soon as I’ve towel-dried,” says Levy. To top it off, she always carries a portable body oil or travel-sized fragrance for touch-ups on her pulse points throughout the day. “This allows you to refresh with the same fragrance or layer on another.” Her current favorite is Costa Brazil Aroma in Oil, which blends green leaves, woody notes, and lush tropical florals.

Lastly, Iso E Super

My beauty editor peers who are fragrance enthusiasts swear by one particular note for making them smell effortlessly amazing all day: Iso E Super. This fragrance molecule adapts to your own scent chemistry, smelling unique on everyone, but it always remains clean and musky — like your favorite sweater. It’s best worn on skin, especially pulse points, where your body heat helps amplify the scent as the day goes on. Escentric Molecules built its entire line around Iso E Super, but now other brands like Commodity are embracing the molecule, too.
